## The shape

A test drives a piece of shared infrastructure. The test is CORRECT — it isolates its own
inputs properly, builds a throwaway fixture root, asserts the right thing, and passes. But the
code under test has a side-effect on **process-global state**, and that side-effect is not
covered by the test's isolation. The write lands in production state, keyed only by data the
fixture chose.

Downstream, a consumer reads that state. It has no field that distinguishes "measured against
the real tree" from "measured against a fixture in `/tmp`", so it treats the record as genuine
and acts on it.

The tell: **an artifact that refers to something that has never existed.**

## Measured case (EI-21985631427355996)

`tsc-red-sweep` files a work-item when a committed tsc red persists past a 45-minute dwell
threshold — deliberately conservative, because most such reds self-heal. It filed:

> Standing tsc red with no owner: `lib/old-peer.ts` (173min, 1 errors)

`find . -name 'old-peer*'` returns nothing. The path has never existed in the repository.

The chain:

1. `lint-tsc.test.ts` builds a fixture repo with `mkdtempSync()`, writes `lib/old-peer.ts` into
   it, and drives the tsc baseline gate against that root. Entirely reasonable.
2. The gate's hot path calls `recordStandingReds({ entries, project })` — no `path`, no `root`
   — which appends to `DEFAULT_OBSERVATION_PATH`, one process-global JSONL store. The paths it
   writes are relative to whatever root the gate ran from.
3. `tscRedSweep` reads that store, sees `lib/old-peer.ts` observed 10 times across 172 minutes,
   applies the dwell decision, and files a `major` bug.

One run of that one test moved the store from 11 to 12 `old-peer` records. Fifteen accumulated.

Two properties made it worse than a stray record:

- **The phantom outranked real work.** `selectDwelledReds` sorts by dwell, and the sweep caps
  filings at `MAX_FILES_PER_TICK`. A long-lived fixture path therefore consumes a slot that a
  genuine standing red needed.
- **It could never auto-close.** `decideTscRedCleared` deliberately refuses to resolve on a
  vanished file ("ambiguous: deleted or renamed") — correct, because a rename carries a red to a
  new path. So the false item was permanently stuck.

## Why per-test discipline is the wrong fix

The tempting remedy is to make the test point the store somewhere else. Reject it: 10+ suites
here drive this gate, and the eleventh will forget. A rule that must be remembered at every call
site has already failed — it is the hand-maintained rung of the derived-truth ladder.

**Scope the record to the tree it was measured against, and let the reader discard what is not
its own.** Nobody has to remember anything.

```js
// write: stamp the root the entries are relative to
recordStandingReds({ entries, project, root });

// read: drop lines stamped with a DIFFERENT tree
if (root && typeof rec.root === 'string' && rec.root && rec.root !== root) continue;
```

**Make the filter asymmetric on purpose.** An UNSTAMPED line means *unknown*, not *foreign*, and
must be admitted — a reader that discarded unknowns would silently blind itself to every legacy
record and to any caller that genuinely cannot name its root. Act only on positive evidence that
a record belongs to some other tree.

## The second guard: a filing precondition

Scoping fixes the source. Also guard the consumer, because the next pollution source will not be
this one. Here the precondition is almost tautological once stated: **tsc cannot report an error
for a file that is not in the tree**, so a dwelled path that does not exist is not a red this
tree can have.

Notably, the mechanism already existed. `fileExistsFn` was already declared on the shared
`TscRedSweepDeps` and already consumed by the RESOLVE pass. It had simply never been applied on
the FILING pass — the recurring "the guard exists, its application is too narrow" shape. Grep the
honouring path before building anything.

Place it **before** the cap, or the phantom still consumes a slot before being discarded.

## Opening and closing have opposite polarities — do not "harmonize" them

A reviewer will notice that this sweep now refuses to FILE on a missing file while
`decideTscRedCleared` refuses to CLOSE on one, and will read it as an inconsistency. It is not.
They are duals and both are right:

- **Closing** on absence is an absence argument about a red that may have merely moved.
- **Opening** demands positive evidence that there is something to fix.

A rename is still handled correctly: the red is observed again at its new path and files there.
Say this in a comment at both sites, or someone will make them agree and reintroduce one of the
two bugs.

## How to find your own instance

Ask of any hot path that writes durable state: **would this write be distinguishable from a real
one if a test made it?** If the record carries no field naming the world it was measured in, the
answer is no.

Then look for these smells in the consumer's output:

- an artifact naming a path, id, or entity that does not exist;
- a label field that quietly disagrees with its neighbours (here every real record read
  `project: "operator-core"`; the fixture's read `project: "test"` — visible in the data the
  whole time, and the fastest way in);
- an item that cannot be closed by any code path.

The confirmation is cheap and worth doing rather than reasoning about: count the records, run the
suspected test once, count again.
